Interpretable subgroup identification with forestsearch

The German Breast Cancer Study Group analysis of León and Anderson (2026b), Table 1, run end to end

Larry Leon

2026-10-29

Source: vignettes/forestsearch.qmd 
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = "#>", fig.align = "center")
library(forestsearch)
library(survival)

A confirmatory trial is powered for an effect in its whole population, and the indication it supports describes a population in which efficacy and a favourable benefit–risk balance have been concluded. Regulatory guidance asks that this conclusion be examined across relevant subgroups rather than assumed, and that a sub-population in which it does not hold be left out of the indication; it credits a subgroup finding only when credible — tied to prior plausibility and replication — and warns that an estimate singled out for its extremity is biased by the selection (European Medicines Agency 2019). Approvals have been restricted to a subgroup after a positive result in the whole population (Amatya et al. 2021).

A subgroup of concern is reached by searching the trial’s covariates after the data are seen, or by examining many prespecified subgroups and singling one out. Either way it is chosen for the extremity of its estimate, and its effect is reported through the analysis the trial would have run had that subgroup been the only one: the treatment coefficient of the trial’s working model fitted within it, a Cox log hazard ratio for a time-to-event outcome. So chosen, the subgroup carries an estimate that overstates its effect, and the same selection distorts the estimate for the patients outside it. forestsearch is built for this situation.

Identification — what the package searches for, and how

  • Interpretable candidates. Every candidate subgroup is a conjunction of at most two covariate cuts, so whether a patient belongs is read from the patient’s own measurements.
  • Three identifiers, one form. Forest search (León et al. 2024), the causal forest of generalized random forests (GRF; Athey et al. 2019, Cui et al. 2023) and the difference-in-natural-parameters estimator (DINA; Gao and Hastie 2025) each score a family of candidates by an estimated treatment effect, admit those whose standard-analysis estimate β̂(g)\hat\beta(g) clears a threshold common to all three, and return one admitted candidate as a selection rule directs — or none, if none is admitted. Forest search enumerates the candidates exhaustively; DINA and GRF propose them from a surface fitted to the outcome, and every proposal is re-ranked on β̂(g)\hat\beta(g) against the same threshold.
  • The orientation. The search runs in the direction of a sub-optimal effect — the package’s “harm” direction, a hazard ratio above one for a survival outcome — the direction in which the trial’s conclusion of benefit would not hold for the patients concerned.
  • The consistency screen, in closed form. Forest search additionally requires a candidate’s effect to replicate across random half-splits. That screen is complementary-pairs stability selection applied to a smooth estimating-function coefficient, so the replication rate follows in closed form from one fit of the working model within the candidate: nothing is drawn, and the search is deterministic given the data.
  • The selection rule is a modelling choice. The rule moves the returned region along a frontier of size against effect — the largest admitted region, the largest within a band of the strongest effect, the strongest effect itself — and so determines what identification and inference are about.
  • The targets. The region returned is Ĥ\hat H; the targets are β(Ĥ)\beta(\hat H) and, for the patients outside it, β(Ĥc)\beta(\hat H^{c}): the working model’s coefficient in each population, its least-false value whether or not the model is correct, on the scale on which the trial was powered and on which regulators and clinicians read its results.

Inference — what is reported about the identified region, and about the rest of the trial

  • The correction. Refit-free multiplier resampling over the candidate family removes the optimism of selection from the estimate in Ĥ\hat H and in Ĥc\hat H^{c} (León and Anderson 2026a).
  • One-sided bounds, and a claim about both groups. The field inverts the law of the residual the correction leaves into a one-sided lower bound on β(Ĥ)\beta(\hat H); field-s gives the one-sided upper bound on β(Ĥc)\beta(\hat H^{c}), relevant to a benefit claim for the patients outside the subgroup; the Bonferroni pair joins the two in a two-subgroup claim at a joint level. Coverage is asymptotically exact under separated selection, characterized under local competition, and conditional on the family proposed when the family comes from the outcomes (León and Anderson 2026b).
  • Declaration control. Whether a subgroup should be declared at all is governed separately: the law of the maximum over the enumerated family gives the family-wise rate of falsely declaring a subgroup when every candidate’s effect is at least a clinically specified benefit — a diagnostic of the rate the chosen thresholds imply and, where a capped rate is wanted, the calibrated cutoff that holds it (León and Anderson 2026b).
  • Reading. Each estimate and bound is read by its location against the trial’s own effect and against clinically meaningful effect sizes, not as a test at the null. Whether and how to act on a finding is a broader judgement of benefit and risk, which this inference is meant to inform.

This vignette runs the analysis reported as Table 1 of León and Anderson (2026b), on the German Breast Cancer Study Group (GBSG) trial that ships with survival, at the manuscript’s settings: the three identifiers, each by one call; the selection-adjusted analysis of each identified region and its complement; and the declaration calibration at a protected level. The computation takes about a minute on one core; the fit times are printed as they are measured.

The data

The analysis set is the 686 patients with complete prognostic data, out of 720 randomized: 246 received hormonal therapy and 440 did not, with 299 recurrences or deaths. Seven covariates enter the search: age, menopausal status, tumour size, grade, the number of positive lymph nodes, and the progesterone and estrogen receptor concentrations in fmol/l. Randomization status is masked in the distributed data; hormonal therapy is analysed as randomized.

df <- survival::gbsg
df <- within(df, {
  id          <- seq_len(nrow(df))              # the fit's subject identifier
  time_months <- rfstime / 30.4375              # recurrence-free survival, days to months
  grade3      <- ifelse(grade == "3", 1, 0)     # grade 3 against grade 1 or 2
})
confounders <- c("age", "meno", "size", "grade3", "nodes", "pgr", "er")
stopifnot(nrow(df) == 686, sum(df$status) == 299)

whole <- coxph(Surv(time_months, status) ~ hormon, data = df)
whole_hr <- c(est = unname(exp(coef(whole))), exp(confint(whole))[1, ])
c(patients = nrow(df), hormonal_therapy = sum(df$hormon == 1),
  none = sum(df$hormon == 0), events = sum(df$status))
#>         patients hormonal_therapy             none           events
#>              686              246              440              299
sprintf("Whole-trial hazard ratio %.3f (%.3f, %.3f), hormonal therapy vs none",
        whole_hr[["est"]], whole_hr[[2]], whole_hr[[3]])
#> [1] "Whole-trial hazard ratio 0.695 (0.544, 0.888), hormonal therapy vs none"

Every bound below is read against the trial’s own effect, a hazard ratio of 0.695, and against clinically meaningful effect sizes — not as a test at a hazard ratio of one.

The specification

Candidates are conjunctions of at most two covariate cuts (maxk = 2) with more than 60 patients (n.min); forest search additionally requires ten events in each arm (d0.min, d1.min). Continuous covariates take the package’s default cuts, except that the two receptors carry ten candidate cuts each (conf.cont_jcuts) with the value zero — no measured receptor — forced in as a cut of its own (conf_force).

Three thresholds govern the search, on the hazard-ratio scale with harm upward:

  • the screening threshold c1c_1 = hr.threshold, which a candidate’s estimated hazard ratio must clear to be admitted;
  • the per-split threshold c2c_2 = hr.consistency, the claim threshold at which an effect stops being beneficial, which both halves of a random half-split must clear for the split to count as consistent;
  • the consistency level p⋆p^\star = pconsistency.threshold, the proportion of consistent splits a candidate must reach.

The applications of León and Anderson (2026b) set c1=c2=1.0c_1 = c_2 = 1.0 and p⋆=0.90p^\star = 0.90. The splitting-consistency rate is not computed by drawing splits. With consistency_method = "resample" (the default) the rate is evaluated in closed form, as Section 2.2 of that paper gives it: to first order the two half-sample estimates are a mirror pair about the full-sample fit, so the probability that both clear c2c_2 is pcons(g)=2Φ(β̂(g)−log⁡c2σD(g))−1, p_{\mathrm{cons}}(g) \;=\; 2\,\Phi\!\left(\frac{\hat\beta(g) - \log c_2}{\sigma_D(g)}\right) - 1, with σD(g)\sigma_D(g) the scale of the half-sample difference, obtained from the fit’s influence function. Despite its name, "resample" draws nothing. Literal random half-splitting (consistency_method = "split", fs.splits refits per candidate) is retained only as the fallback for a candidate whose closed form cannot be evaluated — a non-convergent fit, for instance — and fs.splits has no effect otherwise. Here every candidate has at least ten events in each arm and the Cox fits converge, so the closed form is evaluable throughout and the search is deterministic given the data. The rate is rounded to pconsistency.digits = 2 decimals before it is compared with p⋆p^\star.

The selection rule is max⁡𝒜N(ε)\max_{\mathcal{A}} N(\varepsilon): among the admitted candidates 𝒜\mathcal{A}, the largest whose hazard ratio is within a fraction ε=0.20\varepsilon = 0.20 of the largest hazard ratio over the family (sg_focus = "effMaxSG", selection_rule = "neighborhood", effect_neighborhood = 0.20). Section 2.1 of León and Anderson (2026b) sets this rule beside the alternatives (max⁡𝒜N\max_{\mathcal{A}} N, max⁡𝒜β̂\max_{\mathcal{A}} \hat\beta, and their smallest-subgroup counterparts), which Figure 1 of that paper draws on this trial’s candidate frontier.

Inference (mr_inference = TRUE): from 5,000 multiplier draws over every size-eligible candidate the identifier proposes, the corrected (two-term) estimate of the effect in the identified region Ĥ\hat H and in its complement Ĥc\hat H^{c} (León and Anderson 2026a); the nominal 95% one-sided field lower bound on β(Ĥ)\beta(\hat H), the field-s upper bound on β(Ĥc)\beta(\hat H^{c}), the studentized complement bound, and the Bonferroni pair, a joint 95% claim on both (León and Anderson 2026b). The field’s own Monte Carlo runs at 1,000 outer and 500 inner draws, the package’s fixed setting on this path. The only randomness in the analysis is in these draws; they are seeded by seedit, so the vignette’s numbers are reproducible.

Forest search

One call. Identification, the unadjusted estimates and every selection-adjusted quantity come out of it together. parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential") keeps the run on one core; the package’s default plan is parallel.

t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fit_fs <- forestsearch(
  df.analysis = df,
  outcome.name = "time_months", event.name = "status", treat.name = "hormon", id.name = "id",
  confounders.name = confounders,
  is.RCT = TRUE, est.scale = "hr", seedit = 8316951,
  # the candidate family
  conf.cont_jcuts = list(er = 10, pgr = 10), conf_force = c("er <= 0", "pgr <= 0"),
  n.min = 60, d0.min = 10, d1.min = 10, maxk = 2,
  # the identifier, its thresholds and the selection rule
  subgroup_method = "consistency", consistency_method = "resample",
  hr.threshold = 1.00, hr.consistency = 1.00, pconsistency.threshold = 0.90,
  stop_threshold = NULL,                      # evaluate every candidate; no early stop
  sg_focus = "effMaxSG", selection_rule = "neighborhood", effect_neighborhood = 0.20,
  # selection-adjusted inference
  mr_inference = TRUE,
  mr_inference_args = list(ci_method = "field", draws = 5000L, include_complement = TRUE,
                           field_scale_complement = "selected", field_decompose = TRUE,
                           keep_declaration_field = TRUE,
                           declaration_c0 = c(0.70, 0.75, 0.80, 0.85)),
  quiet = TRUE, parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential"))
fit_sec_fs <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
g_fs <- fit_fs$mr_inference
cat(sprintf("Identified subgroup: %s\n", paste(fit_fs$sg.harm, collapse = " & ")))
#> Identified subgroup: {er <= 0} & {pgr <= 26}
cat(sprintf("Fit including inference: %.1f s\n", fit_sec_fs))
#> Fit including inference: 33.5 s
cat(sprintf("  multiplier stage %.1f s; field blocks %.1f + %.1f s\n", g_fs$timing_seconds,
            g_fs$field$timing_seconds, g_fs$field$complement$timing_seconds))
#>   multiplier stage 1.1 s; field blocks 16.6 + 2.3 s

The identified region is {er <= 0} & {pgr <= 26}: no measured estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor at most 26 fmol/l. Two arguments in the call are not the defaults and are there for a reason: stop_threshold = NULL has the consistency stage evaluate every screened candidate rather than stop at the first that passes, and field_decompose = TRUE returns the supporting quantities shown below. Everything else that is not the default is the specification itself.

The search in numbers

The fit records how the candidates were whittled down. Supplementary Table S13 of León and Anderson (2026b) reports the same funnel.

counts <- fit_fs$find.grps$filter_counts
funnel <- data.frame(
  stage = c("enumerated (at most two cuts, size-eligible)",
            "fittable (ten events in each arm, Cox fit obtained)",
            "clearing the screening threshold, HR > 1.0",
            "passing the consistency screen, p_cons >= 0.90",
            "re-selection family for inference"),
  candidates = c(counts$n_evaluated, counts$n_passed_cox, counts$n_passed_hr,
                 fit_fs$grp.consistency$n_passed, g_fs$n_family))
knitr::kable(funnel, row.names = FALSE, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
stage candidates
enumerated (at most two cuts, size-eligible) 2,211
fittable (ten events in each arm, Cox fit obtained) 1,410
clearing the screening threshold, HR > 1.0 121
passing the consistency screen, p_cons >= 0.90 9
re-selection family for inference 1,744

The re-selection family is larger than the screened set: multiplier resampling re-selects over every size-eligible candidate under the screening threshold and the consistency screen, without the per-arm event minimum, so the family contains the one the search ranked (Supplementary Section S5).

The candidates that pass the screen, with their size, hazard ratio and consistency rate, are the points of Figure 1 of the paper. The selection rule acts on them.

cand <- as.data.frame(fit_fs$grp.consistency$out_sg$result)
cand$candidate <- ifelse(cand$M.2 == "", cand$M.1, paste(cand$M.1, cand$M.2, sep = " & "))
cand <- cand[order(-cand$N), ]
knitr::kable(cand[, c("candidate", "N", "hr", "Pcons")], digits = 3,
             row.names = FALSE, col.names = c("candidate", "N", "HR", "p_cons"),
             caption = "The candidates passing the consistency screen, largest first.")
The candidates passing the consistency screen, largest first.
candidate N HR p_cons
{er <= 0} 82 1.951 0.96
{er <= 0} & {pgr <= 26} 75 2.222 0.99
{pgr <= 0} & {er <= 9} 71 1.684 0.90
{er <= 0} & {pgr <= 16} 70 1.918 0.95
{er <= 0} & {pgr <= 8} 66 2.129 0.97
{er <= 0} & {pgr <= 2} 62 1.886 0.92
{er <= 0} & {size <= 35} 61 2.537 0.99
{er <= 0} & {nodes <= 7} 61 2.335 0.97
{er <= 0} & !{size <= 20} 61 2.054 0.95 
band <- (1 - 0.20) * max(cand$hr)
within_band <- cand$hr >= band
sel <- cand[within_band, ][which.max(cand$N[within_band]), ]
cat(sprintf("Largest HR over the family: %.2f (N %d). Band: HR >= %.2f.\n",
            max(cand$hr), cand$N[which.max(cand$hr)], band))
#> Largest HR over the family: 2.54 (N 61). Band: HR >= 2.03.
cat(sprintf("max N(eps) takes the largest candidate within the band: N %d, HR %.2f.\n",
            sel$N, sel$hr))
#> max N(eps) takes the largest candidate within the band: N 75, HR 2.22.
cat(sprintf("max N alone would take N %d (HR %.2f); max beta the N %d.\n",
            max(cand$N), cand$hr[which.max(cand$N)], cand$N[which.max(cand$hr)]))
#> max N alone would take N 82 (HR 1.95); max beta the N 61.
stopifnot(sel$N == g_fs$n_selected)   # the rule, re-applied, picks the fit's own selection

All of the passing candidates restrict the estrogen receptor, and the rules differ only in how far that region is trimmed. The max⁡𝒜N(ε)\max_{\mathcal{A}} N(\varepsilon) rule takes the 75 patients with no measured estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor at most 26 fmol/l; max⁡𝒜N\max_{\mathcal{A}} N would take the 82 with no measured estrogen receptor; the effect-maximising rules the 61 with, in addition, tumour size at most 35 mm.

The selection-adjusted analysis of a region

The nine quantities of Table 1 are read from fit$mr_inference. There is no single accessor for them, so the vignette defines one; print(fit) and summary(fit) report the bounds and the diagnostics in their own layout.

table1_column <- function(fit, data) {
  g  <- fit$mr_inference; cc <- g$complement
  fb <- g$field; fc <- fb$complement; js <- fb$joint_s
  in_H <- fit$df.est$treat.recommend[match(data$id, fit$df.est$id)] == 0
  stopifnot(!anyNA(in_H), sum(in_H) == g$n_selected, sum(!in_H) == cc$n)
  f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
  ci <- function(e, l, u) sprintf("%s (%s, %s)", f3(e), f3(l), f3(u))
  c(paste(fit$sg.harm, collapse = " & "),
    sprintf("%d (%d)", sum(in_H), sum(data$status[in_H])),
    ci(g$naive$est, g$naive$lower, g$naive$upper),
    f3(g$debiased$est),
    f3(fb$lower_1s),
    sprintf("%d (%d)", sum(!in_H), sum(data$status[!in_H])),
    ci(cc$naive$est, cc$naive$lower, cc$naive$upper),
    f3(cc$debiased$est),
    f3(fc$upper_1s_s),
    sprintf("%s / %s", f3(js$bonf_lower_H), f3(js$bonf_upper_Hc)))
}
table1_rows <- c("Region", "N (events)", "Unadjusted, 95% CI", "Corrected",
                 "Field, lower bound", "Complement N (events)", "Unadjusted, 95% CI",
                 "Corrected", "Field-s, upper bound", "Bonferroni pair")
knitr::kable(data.frame(row = table1_rows, FS = table1_column(fit_fs, df)),
             col.names = c("", "FS"), row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Forest search: the identified region and its complement.")
Forest search: the identified region and its complement.

The unadjusted hazard ratio in the region is opposite in direction to the trial’s; the correction removes 0.543 on the log scale and leaves 1.276. The field lower bound is the one-sided 95% bound on the region’s effect; the field-s upper bound the one-sided 95% bound on the complement’s; the Bonferroni pair is both at joint 95%, each side at 0.975.

The quantities that support the bounds, as in Supplementary Table S18 of the paper:

fb <- g_fs$field; fc <- fb$complement; js <- fb$joint_s
supporting <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("mean of the simulated selection root, region (log scale)",
               "second-order estimate, region",
               "second-order estimate, complement (field-s)",
               "scale ratio rho_c (field-s vs the unstudentized complement bound)",
               "Bonferroni pair: simulated joint coverage",
               "calibrated split gamma (Bonferroni's own alpha/2 is 0.025)",
               "correlation of the aligned roots"),
  value = c(sprintf("%.3f", fb$lambda_mean), sprintf("%.3f", fb$est2),
            sprintf("%.3f", fc$est2_s), sprintf("%.3f", fc$decomp_fields$scale_ratio_c),
            sprintf("%.4f", js$bonf_joint_prob), sprintf("%.3f", js$gamma),
            sprintf("%.3f", js$corr)))
knitr::kable(supporting, row.names = FALSE)
quantity value
mean of the simulated selection root, region (log scale) -0.022
second-order estimate, region 1.305
second-order estimate, complement (field-s) 0.647
scale ratio rho_c (field-s vs the unstudentized complement bound) 1.002
Bonferroni pair: simulated joint coverage 0.9495
calibrated split gamma (Bonferroni’s own alpha/2 is 0.025) 0.025
correlation of the aligned roots -0.026

The second-order estimate subtracts from the corrected estimate the mean of the simulated selection root; the bound subtracts a quantile of the same law and is not centred on it. A scale ratio near one means field-s and the unstudentized complement bound agree on these data.

The two model-based identifiers

DINA and GRF propose candidates from a surface fitted to the outcome and have them re-ranked on the same Cox coefficient β̂(g)\hat\beta(g) against the same screening threshold; neither applies the consistency screen. Supplementary Section S5 of León and Anderson (2026b) sets the three identifiers side by side, with every setting used here. The selection rule and the inference are the same. The calls differ from forest search’s only in the identifier’s own arguments.

t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fit_dina <- forestsearch(
  df.analysis = df,
  outcome.name = "time_months", event.name = "status", treat.name = "hormon", id.name = "id",
  confounders.name = confounders,
  is.RCT = TRUE, est.scale = "hr", seedit = 8316951,
  conf.cont_jcuts = list(er = 10, pgr = 10), conf_force = c("er <= 0", "pgr <= 0"),
  n.min = 60, d0.min = 10, d1.min = 10, maxk = 2,
  subgroup_method = "dina", dina_select_statistic = "effect",     # DINA's own
  hr.threshold = 1.00, stop_threshold = NULL,
  sg_focus = "effMaxSG", selection_rule = "neighborhood", effect_neighborhood = 0.20,
  mr_inference = TRUE,
  mr_inference_args = list(ci_method = "field", draws = 5000L, include_complement = TRUE,
                           field_scale_complement = "selected", field_decompose = TRUE),
  quiet = TRUE, parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential"))
fit_sec_dina <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fit_grf <- forestsearch(
  df.analysis = df,
  outcome.name = "time_months", event.name = "status", treat.name = "hormon", id.name = "id",
  confounders.name = confounders,
  is.RCT = TRUE, est.scale = "hr", seedit = 8316951,
  conf.cont_jcuts = list(er = 10, pgr = 10), conf_force = c("er <= 0", "pgr <= 0"),
  n.min = 60, d0.min = 10, d1.min = 10, maxk = 2,
  subgroup_method = "grf", grf_selection = "frontier",             # GRF's own
  grf_select_statistic = "effect", grf_depth = 2L, dmin.grf = 0.0, # GRF's own
  hr.threshold = 1.00, stop_threshold = NULL,
  sg_focus = "effMaxSG", selection_rule = "neighborhood", effect_neighborhood = 0.20,
  mr_inference = TRUE,
  mr_inference_args = list(ci_method = "field", draws = 5000L, include_complement = TRUE,
                           field_scale_complement = "selected", field_decompose = TRUE),
  quiet = TRUE, parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential"))
fit_sec_grf <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
g_dina <- fit_dina$mr_inference
g_grf  <- fit_grf$mr_inference
cat(sprintf("DINA: %s  (fit %.1f s; re-selection family %d)\n",
            paste(fit_dina$sg.harm, collapse = " & "), fit_sec_dina,
            g_dina$n_family))
#> DINA: {grade3 >= 1} & {pgr <= 20}  (fit 10.0 s; re-selection family 30)
cat(sprintf("GRF:  %s  (fit %.1f s; re-selection family %d)\n",
            paste(fit_grf$sg.harm, collapse = " & "), fit_sec_grf, g_grf$n_family))
#> GRF:  {er <= 0}  (fit 26.4 s; re-selection family 858)

GRF returns the 82 patients with no measured estrogen receptor, a region that contains forest search’s; DINA returns the 113 who are grade 3 with progesterone receptor at most 20 fmol/l, a different classification. For the two model-based identifiers the candidate family is generated from a surface fitted to the outcome, so their bounds are conditional on the family proposed (Supplementary Section S1.9 of León and Anderson 2026b); forest search’s family is enumerated from the covariates alone.

member <- function(fit) {
  fit$df.est$treat.recommend[match(df$id, fit$df.est$id)] == 0
}
m <- data.frame(FS = member(fit_fs), DINA = member(fit_dina), GRF = member(fit_grf))
partition <- aggregate(cbind(N = 1, events = df$status), by = m, FUN = sum)
knitr::kable(partition[order(-partition$N), ], row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "The three-way partition of the 686 patients by the three selections.")

Field, lower bound 0.634 0.638 0.510
Complement N (events) 611 (258) 573 (238) 604 (254)
Unadjusted, 95% CI 0.605 (0.465, 0.788) 0.641 (0.489, 0.839) 0.615 (0.472, 0.801)
Corrected 0.645 0.658 0.663
Field-s, upper bound 0.804 0.842 0.846
Bonferroni pair 0.509 / 0.840 0.572 / 0.887 0.404 / 0.874

This is Table 1 of León and Anderson (2026b). The calls, the seed and the draw counts are those of the manuscript’s analysis, so the published values are reproduced to the digit; a different draw count would move the corrected estimates and the bounds in the third decimal and leave the regions and the unadjusted estimates unchanged.

Reading the table

Each estimate is read by its location against the trial’s own effect, 0.695; the bounds are reported beside it and are not read as tests at a hazard ratio of one. A corrected estimate above 0.90 is read as suggestive of limited benefit, and where its lower bound lies below 1.0 a benefit cannot be ruled out.

  • Forest search. The unadjusted hazard ratio in its region is 2.222, opposite in direction to the trial’s. The correction leaves 1.276, above 0.90, so suggestive of limited benefit; with a field lower bound of 0.634, below 1.0, a benefit cannot be ruled out. The complement, 89% of the trial, has a corrected estimate of 0.645, a larger benefit than the trial’s, with a field-s upper bound of 0.804.
  • DINA and GRF read the same way: corrected estimates of 1.076 and 1.111 in their regions, with lower bounds below 1.0, and of 0.658 and 0.663 in their complements.
  • The two-subgroup claim. Forest search’s Bonferroni pair is 0.509 for the region and 0.840 for the complement. The complement’s benefit, a hazard reduction of at least 16%, survives the joint adjustment; the region excludes only hazard ratios below 0.509, which is no claim of harm. A claim that the two subgroups differ is not supported; the claim of benefit outside the region is.
  • The substantive reading is the same under all three partitions: a small region whose unfavourable unadjusted estimate the correction largely removes, and a complement, most of the trial, with a corrected benefit larger than the trial’s. With 41 to 61 events in the regions, a claim of harm at a conventional level is not realistic at this trial’s size; the bounds are reported, and how much statistical assurance to require of them is the analyst’s decision in their own setting.

Declaration at a protected level

Every region above was declared at the identifiers’ default settings, forest search’s by the conventional screen at p⋆=0.90p^\star = 0.90. Section 4 of León and Anderson (2026b) asks a different question: would a screen calibrated to protect a clinically meaningful uniform benefit have declared it? The answer is read for forest search, whose family is enumerated. At a protected level c0c_0 and family-wise level α\alpha, the calibrated cutoff κ̂α(c0)\hat\kappa_\alpha(c_0) is the (1−α)(1 - \alpha) quantile of the maximum over the family of each candidate’s standardized statistic T(g)=β̂(g)−log⁡c2σD(g), T(g) \;=\; \frac{\hat\beta(g) - \log c_2}{\sigma_D(g)}, with every candidate shifted to sit at c0c_0, under the law of the fit’s own multiplier draws. The calibrated rule admits a candidate when T(g)≥κ̂α(c0)T(g) \ge \hat\kappa_\alpha(c_0); it holds the family-wise probability of declaring any harm subgroup at α\alpha whenever every candidate’s true effect is c0c_0 or better. fs_declaration_calibration() reads it from the draws the fit above already made (keep_declaration_field = TRUE, with the grid passed as declaration_c0); nothing is redrawn and nothing else in the fit changes.

c0_grid <- c(0.70, 0.75, 0.80, 0.85)
cal    <- fs_declaration_calibration(fit_fs, alpha = 0.10, c0 = c0_grid)
cal_c2 <- fs_declaration_calibration(fit_fs, alpha = 0.10)   # c0 = NULL: the claim threshold
tb <- cal$c0$table
fld <- g_fs$declaration_field
T_H   <- cal$T_hat[[fld$family_id[fld$meta$selected_index]]]
T_max <- max(cal$T_hat)
kappa <- c(tb$kappa_hat, cal_c2$kappa_hat)
declaration <- data.frame(
  c0 = c(sprintf("HR %.2f%s", tb$c0, ifelse(tb$c0 == 0.75, " (primary)", "")),
         "HR 1.00 (claim threshold)"),
  kappa   = sprintf("%.3f", kappa),
  implied = sprintf("%.3f", 2 * pnorm(kappa) - 1),
  fw      = sprintf("%.3f", c(tb$fw_size, cal_c2$fw_size)),
  admits  = c(lengths(cal$c0$admitted_calibrated),
              length(cal_c2$admitted_calibrated)))
knitr::kable(declaration, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrr",
             col.names = c("protected level c0", "kappa-hat", "implied level",
                           "FW size", "admits"),
             caption = paste(
               "Declaration calibration at alpha = 0.10. kappa-hat: the calibrated",
               "cutoff; implied level: 2*Phi(kappa-hat) - 1; FW size: the family-wise",
               "size of the p* = 0.90 screen at c0; admits: candidates the calibrated",
               "rule admits."))
Declaration calibration at alpha = 0.10. kappa-hat: the calibrated cutoff; implied level: 2Phi(kappa-hat) - 1; FW size: the family-wise size of the p = 0.90 screen at c0; admits: candidates the calibrated rule admits.
protected level c0 kappa-hat implied level FW size admits
HR 0.70 2.578 0.990 0.558 0
HR 0.75 (primary) 2.726 0.994 0.667 0
HR 0.80 2.891 0.996 0.769 0
HR 0.85 3.039 0.998 0.844 0
HR 1.00 (claim threshold) 3.503 1.000 0.974 0 
cat(sprintf("T of the declared region: %.3f; largest T in the family: %.3f\n", T_H, T_max))
#> T of the declared region: 2.438; largest T in the family: 2.564
cat(sprintf("The p* = 0.90 screen's cutoff, as the package applies it: %.3f\n", cal$z_pstar))
#> The p* = 0.90 screen's cutoff, as the package applies it: 1.621

The screen’s cutoff is the p⋆=0.90p^\star = 0.90 rule as the package applies it, after the rate is rounded to pconsistency.digits = 2, which is why it sits a little below the 1.645 of an unrounded 0.90.

At the primary protected level, a hazard ratio of 0.75, the calibrated cutoff is 2.726, an implied screening level of 0.994; the region’s statistic is 2.438 and the largest in the family 2.564, so the calibrated screen admits no candidate at that level, and likewise at every protected level on the grid and at the claim threshold. The FW-size column is the diagnostic of the paper’s equation (8): the probability that the p⋆=0.90p^\star = 0.90 screen as executed declares some harm subgroup if every candidate carried a uniform benefit of c0c_0 — a property of this family and covariate design, not the trial’s realized error rate; at the claim threshold it is a boundary size. To run the screen at the implied level, set pconsistency.threshold to it and pconsistency.digits to at least 5, so the level is not rounded away; the package’s pstar_settable and pstar_fine columns in cal$c0$table give what the digit grid can express. The supplement’s Section S1.8.4 adds a realized-rate simulation on this design, which is not run here. The selection and every bound above are those of the fit as run; the calibration reads the fit and alters none of them.

Where to go next

  • The post-selection article reads the bounds in more depth on the same trial: the re-selection frequency p̂ as a diagnostic, membership agreement, and what each construction does and does not say.
  • The package website carries the original workflow of León et al. (2024) — the full argument listing, the bootstrap bias correction and the cross-validation — as the article Exploratory subgroup identification with forestsearch (the 2024 workflow), and the methodology and simulation articles.
  • ?forestsearch documents every argument, with examples for this analysis and for the binary and continuous ACTG 175 analyses of León and Anderson (2026b), and a section on the options not tested against the manuscript analyses.
